data.name: Power War:The First Men
data.detailed_description: Power War – The First Men is a game in first-person multiplayer and it’s create to offer an unique experience in a panoramic of shooter games in continue evolution. The character is an human with special powers, so he is a "superman" with skills hardly findable in other games. His skills, associated with various weapons, and not less the punches, allow the player to move freely within the maps, standing or kneeling and lying on the floor. There are two game modes: the individual experience and team experience (deathmatch and team deathmatch). The teams in the team mode are Zankles e Katane and have the same skills and powers, but different suit's colors. The player has a series of weapons he can use like him prefers. The weapons are assault weapon, an shotgun, sniper and submachine weapon and these are capable to kill the enemy if it is stricken in vital body's part (for example head). Every weapon has a different "power fire" and the damage depends also where the antagonist is stricken.  Furthermore, he has the “grenade” to causes damage to opponent, the "flashes" to blind the antagonist for some second in direct conflict, the "EMPs" that disables the foe's powers, the "smokes" to created a smoke curtain; and more interchangeable attachments: red dot, acog, sniper scope, laser. You will be the protagonist and all depend from your game skill that you will have, having all players same skills and powers. When you have a full control of skills and powers can you quickly movement in all directions, and if necessary when you want, you can use an armor to decrease the damage, so, you can make your gaming experience unique and special, leaving your enemy breathless in front of you.

reviews.review:
Power War: The First Men is a small-scale competitive first-person shooter that tries to put a different spin on traditional gun battles by giving its combatants extraordinary abilities alongside conventional firearms. Developed by Andrea Mancuso and Graziano Ferraro and published by Ferman Studio, it is primarily designed around online player-versus-player action. Rather than building its identity around a lengthy campaign or elaborate story, the game concentrates on direct combat where shooting accuracy, movement, equipment selection, and the intelligent use of powers determine the outcome.

One of its more interesting design decisions is that players operate with the same fundamental supernatural capabilities. Instead of relying on heroes or classes with dramatically different strengths, the game attempts to establish a relatively even starting point. This places greater importance on how effectively players use what they are given. Powers can influence mobility and combat, making firefights less predictable than those of a conventional military shooter. Learning when to rely on firearms and when to exploit special abilities is consequently an important part of becoming effective in battle.

The weapon selection covers familiar FPS categories, including assault-oriented firearms, submachine guns, shotguns, and sniper rifles. Each category encourages a different approach to distance and positioning. Damage also depends on where a target is struck, rewarding accurate shots to vulnerable areas rather than treating every successful hit equally. It is a straightforward system, but it helps preserve the importance of traditional shooting skill even when supernatural abilities are involved. Players can further adjust their weapons with accessories such as red-dot sights, ACOG optics, sniper scopes, and lasers.

Tactical equipment adds another layer to combat. Explosive grenades can punish opponents caught in confined spaces, flash devices interfere with visibility, and smoke can provide concealment when crossing exposed areas or disrupting an opponent's line of sight. EMP equipment has greater significance because it can temporarily interfere with an enemy's powers. This creates a useful counterbalance to the supernatural mechanics. Instead of powers dominating every encounter without resistance, players have a tool capable of forcing opponents back toward conventional combat.

Movement and defensive options contribute to the tactical possibilities as well. Players can fight from standing, crouched, and prone positions while also taking advantage of the enhanced mobility associated with their powers. Armor can reduce incoming damage and provide additional survivability. When these mechanics work together, battles can involve considerably more than exchanging bullets across a room. Positioning, mobility, equipment timing, accuracy, and decisions about when to activate or counter powers all have the potential to influence an encounter.

The available multiplayer modes keep the overall structure uncomplicated. Deathmatch focuses on individual competition, while team deathmatch divides players into opposing sides. The two factions, Zankles and Katane, are visually distinguished but mechanically balanced around equivalent capabilities. This symmetrical approach makes sense for competitive fairness, although it sacrifices some variety. Players who enjoy learning distinct characters, faction-specific equipment, or specialized classes will not find that degree of asymmetry here.

The limited scope is ultimately one of the game's biggest drawbacks. There are several mechanics to experiment with during combat, but the modes surrounding those mechanics are comparatively basic. Without an extensive progression structure, large assortment of activities, or substantial single-player component, repetition can become noticeable. The game's central formula therefore needs to be enjoyable enough to carry the experience on its own.

Its dependence on multiplayer participation is another important consideration. Power War: The First Men is fundamentally designed around encounters with other players, so the experience is heavily affected by the availability of an active community. For a niche multiplayer title, finding populated matches can be a much larger obstacle than the actual learning curve. Players considering it primarily as a solo game should be aware that it does not offer the kind of extensive offline content that could compensate for a limited online population.

Presentation is functional rather than spectacular. The game clearly comes from a much smaller production environment than mainstream competitive shooters, and this can be seen in its overall level of polish and breadth of content. Its most appealing quality is therefore the concept rather than technical extravagance. Combining firearms, melee attacks, tactical grenades, armor, customizable sights, enhanced movement, and supernatural powers gives the combat its personality, even if these ideas are housed within a relatively modest package.

Steam Deck compatibility is officially listed as Unsupported. Players primarily interested in experiencing it on Valve's handheld should keep this limitation in mind rather than assuming that the simple controls automatically guarantee full compatibility. Its design may appear ideal for portable play, but the official Deck classification does not currently provide that assurance.

Overall, Power War: The First Men contains an interesting competitive FPS concept that never quite grows into a fully developed experience. Equalized supernatural powers create a potentially fair foundation, while guns, equipment, EMP counters, armor, different combat stances, and enhanced mobility provide a reasonable collection of tactical tools. Its weaknesses are mainly the narrow selection of activities, modest production quality, reliance on online participation, and limited long-term variety. As an experimental indie shooter it has some worthwhile ideas, but those ideas are easier to appreciate than the complete package is to recommend.

Rating: 5/10
